content.title: About
content.content: Chili is a spicy sauce made from tomatoes, chili peppers and spices, specially formulated for vegetarians. It contains no meat, fish or seafood, yet delivers the rich, piquant flavor typical of traditional chili.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The heat comes from capsaicin, the active compound in chili peppers.
Vegetarian versions often include beans or tofu to boost protein content.
Tomatoes used in the sauce are a great source of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Chili pairs well with Mexican dishes but also works great on pasta, rice and vegetable plates.
There are many heat levels – from mild to extreme ghost‑pepper heat.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Capsaicin may increase metabolic rate and help burn calories.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes and peppers provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Antioxidant source
items.content: Lycopene and other phytochemicals protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Capsaicin can promote vasodilation and improve circulation.

items.title: Plant‑based protein
items.content: Added beans or tofu raise the protein content, important for vegetarians.

items.title: Spiciness
items.content: Very hot sauce may irritate the stomach or esophagus in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some people are allergic to tomatoes or peppers.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain high salt levels; people with hypertension should watch portions.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Capsaicin can enhance the effects of certain anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add chili to vegetarian tacos, burritos, soups, stews, pasta, rice dishes and vegetable casseroles. For milder heat, thin the sauce with plant‑based yogurt or milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in a sealed jar in the refrigerator for up to 4 weeks. For longer storage, freeze in small containers.

green-peas-canned-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Green peas, canned, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Canned green peas are cooked snap peas that retain their bright green color, sweet flavor, and slight crunch after processing. No fat is added during canning, making the product low‑calorie and rich in plant protein, fiber, vitamins, and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peas belong to the legume family and are one of the oldest cultivated crops.
Canning preserves most of the nutrients even after long shelf life.
In the United States canned peas are a staple in classic dishes such as pea soup and salads.
Peas contain natural antioxidants – flavonoids and carotenoids – that give them their vivid color.
Without added fat, canned peas contain less than 80 kcal per 100 g.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of canned peas provides about 8 g of protein, useful for vegetarians and athletes.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of vitamin C and vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity, while vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the product suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often contain added salt for preservation; people monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes, including peas.

items.title: Bacterial spoilage if improperly stored
items.content: Damaged or opened cans left at room temperature for extended periods can lead to spoilage.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peas can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, soups, stews, or used as a sandwich filling. Before serving, drain the liquid and rinse the peas with cold water if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep peas in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 3–4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Lentils are dried legumes harvested from the seeds of the plant Lens culinaris. Grown in temperate regions worldwide, dried lentils contain no added fat and provide a rich source of plant protein, fiber, vitamins, and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lentils are one of the oldest cultivated crops, used in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia.
Several varieties exist – green, brown, red, yellow, and black – each with distinct flavor and cooking time.
Lentils can fix nitrogen in the soil, improving fertility without synthetic fertilizers.
Unlike many beans, lentils do not require pre‑soaking, though it shortens cooking time.
In India lentils are the base of dal, while in the Mediterranean they appear in salads and soups.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Dried lentils contain about 25 g of protein per 100 g, making them a valuable plant‑based protein source.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Provides iron and folate
items.content: Iron is essential for oxygen transport, while folate is crucial for DNA synthesis and anemia prevention.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Lentils raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Contains magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals support heart, muscle, and nervous system function.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to lentils.

items.title: Anti‑nutrient content
items.content: Raw lentils contain phytic acid and lectins that can hinder mineral absorption; cooking neutralizes them.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Some people may experience increased flatulence; gradual introduction can reduce this effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lentils can be boiled, stewed, added to soups, stews, salads, and veggie patties. Rinse them before cooking and optionally soak for 30 minutes to speed up cooking. They pair well with vegetables, spices, meat, and whole grains.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried lentils in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly kept, they remain good for up to 2 years. Discard any lentils that develop a moldy odor or discoloration.

rice-brown-with-dark-green-vegetables-no.title: Brown rice with dark green vegetables, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain product obtained from the whole rice kernel after removing only the outer husk. The dish includes dark green vegetables (such as broccoli, spinach, green peas) and is prepared without added fat, making it low‑calorie and nutrient‑dense.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, so it contains more fiber, vitamins, and minerals than white rice.
Dark green vegetables are rich in chlorophyll, giving them their characteristic color and antioxidant properties.
Because no fat is added, the dish is low in calories while still providing satiety through fiber and protein.
Brown rice has a lower glycemic index than white rice, helping to stabilize blood sugar levels.
When stored properly, whole brown rice can stay fresh for up to 6 months.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes a feeling of fullness, and helps maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of magnesium and selenium
items.content: These minerals are essential for muscle function, nervous system health, and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is important for amino‑acid metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Helps control blood glucose, beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Antioxidants from green vegetables
items.content: Lutein, zeaxanthin and other phytochemicals protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid in whole grains can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting the rice can mitigate this.

items.title: Arsenic in rice
items.content: Rice may contain trace amounts of arsenic; choose reputable brands and vary grains in the diet.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: Rare but possible; individuals with a rice allergy should avoid the product.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish as a standalone meal or as a side. It pairs well with lean protein such as grilled chicken, fish, or tofu, and can be added to salads. Cook the rice by steaming, add the vegetables at the end of cooking to keep them crisp and vibrant.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry brown rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked portions should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 3‑4 days and reheated thoroughly before serving.
